question: In the pulverized-coal boiler, what ammonia flow rate is used in the cofiring case whose coal feeding rate is 20.33 kg/s?
rendered:
<document title="Ammonia Co-Firing in a Staged-Air Pulverized-Coal Boiler: Reactor-Network Prediction of Carbon Reduction and Nitrogen-Oxide Emissions">

=== page 1 ===
- In this work, a Chemkin-based chemical reactor network (CRN) is developed for a 350 MW pulverized-coal boiler with staged air, combining perfectly stirred reactors for the main furnace zones with detailed gas-phase kinetics and heterogeneous NO-char/soot reactions.
- The CRN is validated against staged drop-tube-furnace measurements for pure coal and 20% ammonia cofiring (dry 6%O2), predicting outlet O2, CO2 and CO within ∼10% and capturing the measured NO rise.
- With ammonia introduced in the flame zone, simulations for 0−80% blending (20% step) show near-linear reductions in CO2 and CO (−21%/−73% at 20%; −84%/−98% at 80%), while char consumption is delayed and the NO/burnout peaks shift downstream.
- NO varies nonlinearly, increasing from 20% to 60% but decreasing at 80%.
- At 20% cofiring, injection location is critical: postflame injection minimizes CO2/CO (−33%/−80%) but increases NO (∼+88%), whereas burnout-zone injection causes a much larger NO penalty (about +571%).
- Among the 20% cofiring cases, flame-zone injection yields the lowest predicted NO emission.
- With global greenhouse-gas emissions at record highs and the emissions gap still unclosed, immediate, unprecedented and sustained mitigation is now essential to limit climate risks and keep returning to 1.5 °C by 2100 within the realm of possibility.^1 Coal still supplies just over one-third of global electricity generation, so decarbonizing existing coal boilers remains a near-term priority.^2−4 Ammonia cofiring offers a potential route to reduce direct CO2 emissions from existing pulverized-coal boilers by replacing part of the coal-derived thermal input with a carbon-free fuel.^5−7 Its application, however, requires attention to both fuel conversion and nitrogen-oxide emissions.

=== page 2 ===
- At the mechanistic level, NO production in NH3-containing flames is governed by a radical-sensitive oxidation network in which NH3 is converted through NH2/NH/N intermediates, and the competition between N2-forming and NO-forming channels depends strongly on the local H/O radical pool and the flame structure.^9 Detailed-mechanism analyses identify the HNO route as a major contributor to NO formation over wide condition ranges, which makes OH-related reactions and residence time in high-temperature zones high-leverage sensitivities for NO prediction and control.^9−11,13,14 Previous studies have examined ammonia−coal cofiring under different blending ratios and air-staging conditions.
- This motivates an examination of the temperature, species evolution, and nitrogen-reaction pathways in individual furnace zones as the ammonia blending ratio changes.^15,19,20 Recent high-fidelity numerical studies have further clarified the roles of multistream mixing and species transport in pulverized-coal/ammonia flames.
- Wen et al. developed a four-fuel-stream flamelet model for large-eddy simulation that separately represents coal volatiles, char off-gases, ammonia, and the pilot stream.^21 Their subsequent carrier-phase direct numerical simulation identified distinct coal- and ammonia-dominated reaction regions and showed that, for the flame investigated, NO was formed mainly in the coal-dominated region, with volatile-N species making an important con-tribution.^22 Later flamelet-based large-eddy simulations and carrier-phase direct numerical simulations further showed that differential diffusion can affect local thermochemical quantities and NOx distributions, while its inclusion improves the prediction of temperature and NOx mass fractions in the flamelet framework.^23,24 These findings provide a flame-scale basis for interpreting why changes in ammonia blending ratio and injection location can alter nitrogen-conversion behavior in the present zonal model.
- Ammonia-derived nitrogen can proceed through competing NO-forming and N2-forming pathways, while reactions involving char and soot provide additional routes for NO consumption.^25,30,31 Chemical reactor networks offer a tractable approach for incorporating detailed chemistry into a zonal representation of boiler combustion.^25,32−34 By representing furnace regions as interconnected ideal reactors, a CRN allows the evolution of temperature and species to be examined along a prescribed reaction sequence.
- In this study, a CHEMKIN-based CRN is developed for a 350 MW pulverized-coal boiler with staged air, incorporating detailed gas-phase chemistry and heterogeneous reactions involving char and soot.
- At constant total fuel thermal input and with a prescribed air-staging arrangement, ammonia thermal shares of 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, and 80% are first investigated with ammonia supplied to the flame zone.
- Ammonia injection into the flame zone, postflame zone, and burnout zone is then compared at a thermal share of 20%.

Answer: 
The ammonia flow rate used in the cofiring case whose coal feeding rate is 20.33 kg/s is 10.29 m^3/s.
